newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Better days seen as Manila GNP exceeds forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Better days seen as Manila GNP exceeds forecasts.

text.p: The Philippines is reaping the benefits of economic reform and political stability with strong first-half growth in 1996 fuelling hopes it will exceed official targets in the next three years, economists said on Saturday.
Their comments follow the release of figures by the National Statistics Coordination Board which showed gross national product (GNP) grew 7.06 percent in the first six months of 1996.
This was much stronger than most expectations and compares with a rate of 5.16 percent in the same period last year.
Second-quarter GNP growth was 7.69 percent, the best quarterly result since January-March 1990, acting socio-economic planning secretary Raphael Lotilla told a news conference.
"We have to sit down and ... see what these numbers imply for our full-year projection," National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) deputy director general Dante Canlas said.
A recent Reuter poll showed that most analysts were expecting only 6.4 percent GNP growth for the first six months.
The government has forecast 6.5-7.5 percent GNP growth for the whole of 1996, up from 5.7 percent last year, and a rise to 7.0-8.0 percent in 1997 and 8.5 percent in 1998.
"The results of the first semester of 1996 provide grounds for optimism that we'll be able to meet these targets or even exceed them," Canlas added.
Emilio Neri, an economist at the University of Asia and Pacific, said his institution's forecast for 6.6 percent internal growth this year could easily be attained.
A continued slowdown in inflation and interest rates would further strengthen the foundations for steady growth over the next three years, he added.
Economists expect August inflation, due to be announced next week, to continue falling despite an oil price increase triggered by partial deregulation of the energy sector.
Lotilla attributed the steady growth to political stability and economic reforms in the Philippines, once regarded as a lost cause in a region of booming economies.
"The past economic reforms in an environment of enhanced peace and political stability are beginning to bear fruit," he said.
Apart from restoring political stability, President Fidel Ramos's government has opened basic industries to foreign competition and dismantled inefficient monopolies.
"The economy now is linked to the rest of the world ... Filipinos here are able to invest abroad. You will see that there is an increasing share of income from overseas investments," Canlas said.
Remittances from abroad grew by a hefty 76.5 percent in the first half of the year.
Gross domestic product grew by 5.05 percent in the first six months compared to 4.7 percent a year ago, with the services and industry sectors contributing to the growth.
The agriculture sector, which suffered from prolonged drought only to be hit by a series of typhoons last year, produced 6.0 percent growth in the first half of 1996.
